procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 17th day of April 1953 of the Nagpur High Court in Miscellaneous Civil Case No. 53 of 1950.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Income-tax Appellate Tribunal, Bombay Branch 'A' referred a question to the High Court under section 66(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act XI of 1922. The High Court answered the referred question against the appellant.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant applied to the High Court under section 66-A(2) of the Act for a certificate for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court, but this was dismissed. The appellant then obtained special leave to appeal from the Supreme Court on December 6, 1954.

decision.appeal_result: this appeal should be dismissed with costs

issue.issue_text: Whether the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was legally competent to direct the Income-tax Officer to register a firm after obtaining the signature of a partner on both the application for registration and the deed of partnership.

facts: A firm's application for registration was rejected by the Income-tax Officer because one partner, Gokulchand, had not signed the application or the partnership deed.
On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner (AAC) cancelled the rejection and directed the Income-tax Officer to register the firm after obtaining Gokulchand's signature on both documents.
The Supreme Court decided the case on the factual basis that a properly signed application (with Gokulchand's signature) was not before the AAC when he made his order.
law: The governing law is Rule 2 of the Indian Income-tax Rules, 1922.
Rule 2 requires an application for registration to be signed by all partners personally.
Rule 2(c) defines the power of the AAC in an appeal: he can permit the appellant to make a proper application, signed by all partners, to the Income-tax Officer before the assessment is finalized.
application: The Court reasoned that the power granted to the AAC under Rule 2(c) was limited to one specific action: according permission to file a correctly completed application.
The AAC did not have the authority to direct the Income-tax Officer to perform a future act, such as obtaining a signature, and then register the firm.

The order issued by the AAC went beyond the scope of his legal competence as defined by the Rule. Since no properly signed application was before him, the only power he had was to allow one to be submitted, which he did not do.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was not legally competent to direct the Income-tax Officer to register the firm after obtaining the missing signature. The Court held that Rule 2(c) of the Indian Income-tax Rules did not grant the AAC the power to issue such a directive, and therefore the High Court's decision to reject this power was correct.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was legally competent to direct the Income-tax Officer to register a firm after obtaining the signature of a partner on both the application for registration and the deed of partnership.
appellant_arguments: The appellant contended that a valid application, signed by all partners (including the one in jail), had in fact been filed with the Appellate Assistant Commissioner (AAC).

It was argued that the AAC's order directing registration was therefore proper, and the additional instruction to the Income-tax Officer to 'obtain the signature' should be treated as superfluous or unnecessary.
The appellant cited previous partnership deeds which provided for the continuation of the firm even upon the death or retirement of a partner to support the firm's ongoing validity.
It was also argued that it is not legally necessary for all partners to sign the partnership agreement for it to be registered, as long as the non-signing partner had assented to it.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, upheld by the Tribunal, was that no valid application signed by all partners was ever submitted to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner (AAC).
Under Rule 2(c) of the Indian Income-tax Rules, 1922, the AAC's power is limited to granting permission for a properly signed application to be submitted to the Income-tax Officer.
The AAC has no legal authority or power to direct the Income-tax Officer to obtain the missing signatures and then register the firm; such a directive is beyond the scope of the rules.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under Rule 2(c) of the Indian Income-tax Rules, 1922, an Appellate Assistant Commissioner is only empowered to permit the filing of a registration application duly signed by all partners before the assessment is finalized. The rule does not confer the legal authority to direct an Income-tax Officer to register a firm after obtaining a missing partner's signature on the application and the partnership deed.
obiter: The court declined to express an opinion on whether a partnership agreement is admissible for registration if it is not signed by all partners, but a non-signing partner has assented to it and put it forward for registration.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: On the question as framed, the only answer which the High Court could give was that the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was not legally competent to direct the Income-tax Officer to register the firm after obtaining the signature of Gokulchand both in the application for registration and in the deed of partnership. Rule 2(c) above-quoted did not empower the Appellate Assistant Commissioner to do anything of the sort and we are of the opinion that the answer given by the High Court in the negative was, therefore, correct.
legal_tests_applied: Under Rule 2(c) of the Indian Income-tax Rules, 1922, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had only the power to direct registration of the firm if an application duly signed by all the partners had been presented to him before the assessment was confirmed, reduced, enhanced or annulled.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellant's factual contention that a valid application signed by all partners was ever filed with the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, stating, 'As appears abundantly clear from the terms of the order made by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner himself and also from the statement of case prepared by the Tribunal, the application signed by all the partners personally including Gokulchand was not before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner.'

The court was 'not impressed' with the appellant's argument that the directive to obtain a signature should be treated as superfluous, as this argument was contingent on the existence of a validly signed application, which the court found was not present.

The court dismissed the appellant's reference to earlier partnership deeds as irrelevant, stating, 'We fail to understand what bearing these clauses have on the determination of the referred question.'
why_respondent_won: The court agreed with the respondent's interpretation of the law, finding that the Appellate Assistant Commissioner's powers under Rule 2(c) are limited and do not include directing an Income-tax Officer to obtain missing signatures.

The court accepted the respondent's factual position, which was supported by the record, that no valid application signed by all partners was available to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner at the time of the hearing.
